item.content:encoded:
It's a great article, but I don't really understand why any Foundation researchers would be willing to risk their careers and possibly even lives in order to steal this meme just to release it to a random village in Bangladesh? What was their motivation? Did they think they were helping people be releasing the meme?

Because surely every Foundation researcher must realize that the Foundation doesn't just erase people's memories to maintain normalcy and their own operational secrecy - they also do it as a mercy. With all the horrifically traumatizing and outright insanity causing anomalies in existence, there has got to be plenty of people out there who are only able to continue functioning normally because they were subjected the Foundation's amnestics. Even more so among the Foundation's own employees than the general populace! I'd imagine that if you were to apply this meme to any random person in the world, there would be a not-insignificant chance that the moment the secondary symptoms kicked in they would collapse into a nervous wreck, relapse into insanity and/or commit suicide ASAP. There are people who will *die* if forced to remember everything they have ever experienced.

Really, as long as this meme can spread uncontrollably, releasing it from containment would highly unethical - not only would it be a massive security breach and likely cause riots and widespread social upheaval from the existence of anomalies becoming public knowledge, it would also be incredibly cruel to all those people who have been exposed to nightmarish, psyche-destroying abominations that they are better off not remembering.

item.title: Re: +100
item.content:encoded:
There's a condition called "hyperthymesia" which, in practice, is what we think of as perfect memory. Basically, if they remembered something, they won't ever forget it.

They have issues with personal relationships (they're ALWAYS correct, and that can have a negative impact with others), as well as having difficulties with the day-to-day (they can recall memories withput concious effort. If they suddenly remember that head-on they were in ten years back in vivid detail while driving…)

item.title: Re: +100
item.content:encoded:
I upvoted it years ago. Keep trying every time I end up here. This is such a launching point for thought. The blessing of perfect memory. The curse of not being able to forget.

One thing I always wondered about were the long-term effects. Nothing comes without a price. We unlock a superior recall system. What's the wear-and-tear (MTBF) of the rest of the brain? Do they wake up suddenly unable to remember anything thirty-seven years (+/- 2%) later?? Or is it like the final effect from Flowers for Algernon, where you watch your brain dying in hopeless horror?

Either way, congrats!

Or +101, rather. It crept up for weeks, and now it gets two votes in a day? I missed it ;~;

This is the first piece I ever posted that didn't get deleted for low rating, four years ago minus six days (couldn't've waited? >.>). I wouldn't have believed anyone if they told me it would ever hit +100, and I still wouldn't have until it got to +85 or something. I still don't know whether it deserves it.

I vaguely want to make some sappy speech about my time here and thanking people and such, but that's too much effort and also not really my style.

*twirls noisemaker*

item.title: Author's note
item.content:encoded:
Since the topic of anti-memes has been coming up more and more lately: I headcanon 868 as a "counter" to the types of forgetting characteristic of normal human experience. Foundation-used amnestics typically target/accelerate these same processes, and are thus nullified. AMN-868 operates on different principles, and can thus ignore SCP-868's innoculation and destroy it.

Different anti-memes, depending on what mechanisms they use to influence memory, may or may not be affected by SCP-868. I like to imagine that a number of them would be, but we would really have no idea of telling.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Very nice, read this before joining, but just reread, and +1.

A couple thoughts:
1) There are reasonably well supported theories that our brains forget for a reason, and that it is one of the processes that keep us functioning as we do. You already pointed out that we would remember every bad instance, but negative and positive bias become meaningless when you can't forget any example. For as good case study as you'll probably find IRL, look at Solomon Shereshevsky Here's a good link. If long term operation under the influence of SCP-868 were possible, the resultant mind might not be human as we know it.

2) There are so many majorly dangerous memetic and infohazard SCPs that haven't been too dangerous to leave on the books, that I think containment loss of SCP-868, especially within the Foundation, might qualify as a Keter class event. The Foundation would have to be insanely careful when screening the screeners of the screeners of the personnel to be exposed to SCP to make certain that it wouldn't uncover anything too dangerous.

3) A crazy long-shot idea (that between thinking of and typing I realized owes heavily to Marvel's Wolverine), but would SCP-868 uncover information lost in a reality restructuring event, or even a small subset of reality restructuring events? This could make it even more useful/ disastrous!

I put them in because the 2000 contest is showing that people can get away with articles that don't identify with the object class trinary.

The latin bits roughly translate to some aspect of the entry. There's no hard-and-fast rule for it other than what I thought would sound cool. In this case, 'nuntii' translates to 'news' (according to google translate), which means that SCP-868 transfers information.

For those of you wondering, I appended a latin suffix to the object classes of all of my SCPs. Hopefully this encourages other established authors to do their own thing with object classes too, rather than just making me "that guy who makes latin object classes".
